title: What would you put behind a CDN, and what wouldn't you?
summary: Tests scope: CDNs are for cacheable, publicly shareable content — can you draw that line correctly for personalized or write-heavy paths?

slides.markdown:
"Just CDN it" is the reflex this question is testing against — a CDN is fantastic for the right content and actively dangerous for the wrong content. A CDN serves the **same cached bytes** to many users from an edge location near them; that's only safe when the bytes really are the same for everyone.

The strong answer draws the line explicitly: static, shared, cacheable GETs go to the CDN; anything personalized, write, or auth-gated stays at the origin.

Ask: **is this content the same for every user, or personalized per request?** This is the single question that decides CDN-eligibility. A logo, a JS bundle, a blog post body — identical for everyone, safe to cache at the edge. A dashboard, a personalized feed, anything behind a login that varies by who's asking — not safe to cache at a shared edge layer without extra care.

Get this wrong and the CDN either does nothing useful or actively serves one user's data to another.

State the rule: **CDN for static, shared, cacheable GET requests; origin for personalized, write, or auth-gated requests.** GETs are cacheable by nature (they shouldn't have side effects); writes never belong at the CDN because they must reach the origin to take effect. Auth-gated responses are excluded even if they're GETs, because "same URL, different response per user" is exactly the shape a CDN handles badly by default.

This one rule covers nearly every case you'll be asked to classify.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: images and JS bundles vs a personalized dashboard
slides.markdown:
| | Images & JS bundles | Personalized dashboard API response |
|---|---|---|
| Same for every user? | Yes — identical bytes | No — varies by logged-in user |
| Cacheable at CDN? | Yes, aggressively, often for days | No, not directly |
| Right home | CDN edge | Origin, or a per-user cache at the app layer |

**How to decide:** ask what breaks if the CDN serves the exact same cached response to two different users hitting the same URL. For images, nothing breaks. For the dashboard, one user sees another's data — an immediate correctness and security failure.

Two headers do the real work of telling a CDN what's safe to cache and for whom. **Cache-Control** says whether a response can be cached at all and for how long (`public, max-age=3600` vs `private, no-store`). **Vary** tells the CDN which request headers make the response different — `Vary: Accept-Encoding` is common and harmless, but a response that actually differs per user (say, based on a cookie or auth header) needs that reflected in `Vary`, or explicitly marked `private` so the CDN never caches it as shared at all.

Getting these two headers right is the entire mechanism that keeps a CDN safe.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: a mostly-static blog page with a live comment count
slides.markdown:
A blog post's body, title, and images are cached at the CDN with a **1-hour TTL** — they rarely change, and any reader gets the identical bytes. The **live comment count**, which changes constantly, is fetched separately by a small client-side request that hits the origin directly, bypassing the CDN cache entirely.

This is the same fragmenting idea from the "what to cache" question, applied at the CDN layer: split the page into a cacheable shell and a live piece, rather than deciding cacheable-or-not for the whole page.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
| Caching more at the CDN | Caching less at the CDN |
|---|---|
| Cuts origin load and latency hardest for users far from the origin | Origin serves every request directly, cost and latency scale with traffic |
| Every cached response is a staleness window you now own | No staleness risk, but no relief for global users either |

**How to decide:** CDN caching pays off most for users geographically far from your origin, but every response you cache there is a staleness commitment — you're promising it's safe to serve that exact response to anyone, for however long the TTL says, so only make that promise for content that's genuinely the same for everyone.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "can you CDN a mostly-static page with one personalized widget?"
slides.markdown:
Yes — via **edge includes or fragment caching**: the CDN caches the static shell of the page normally, and a small marked region (an include) is fetched fresh per request and stitched in at the edge before the response reaches the user. The personalized widget never gets cached; everything around it does.

This is the CDN-layer version of the same fragmenting pattern seen throughout this group — the answer to "can you cache a mixed page" is almost always "split it," not "cache it all or none of it."

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "a misconfigured Vary header just leaked one user's page to another"
slides.markdown:
This is a real, serious class of bug — a cached response meant for user A gets served to user B because the CDN wasn't told the response varies by something user-specific. Catching it requires two things: **automated tests that assert cache headers on personalized endpoints** (fail the build if a response missing `private` or a correct `Vary` header is cacheable), and **monitoring for cache hit rates on endpoints that should never be cacheable** — a nonzero hit rate there is a direct signal something is wrong.

Naming this as a security bug, not just a caching bug, is the right framing — it's a data leak, not a performance issue.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: trying to CDN an authenticated per-user API response
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This API response is a GET, so it's safe to cache at the CDN like everything else."

**Why it's wrong:** being a GET only means it *should* be side-effect-free — it says nothing about whether the response is the same for every caller. An authenticated, per-user API response varies by who's asking, so caching it at a shared edge layer risks serving one user's private data to another the next time the same URL is requested.

**Correct model:** GET-ness is necessary but not sufficient for CDN caching — also require that the response doesn't vary by user, or explicitly scope the cache per user (and know that per-user CDN caching is unusual and rarely worth it compared to an app-layer cache).

CDN for static, shared, cacheable GETs; origin for personalized, write, or auth-gated requests. Cache-Control and Vary are the mechanism that keeps this safe — get them wrong and a CDN can leak one user's response to another, a security bug, not just a caching bug. Mixed pages get fragmented — a cached shell plus a live or personalized piece fetched separately — rather than an all-or-nothing decision. Monitor cache hit rates on endpoints that should never be cacheable as a tripwire for this exact failure.
